query: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs phase stability and why, with relevance to retaining desirable combinations of high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness? Specify a controlled comparison, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries of the hypothesis, supporting prior evidence, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high‐entropy alloys, an optimal (partial) degree of local chemical ordering—manifested as the formation of nanoscale, coherent B2 precipitates within a primarily disordered FCC matrix—controls phase stability. This intermediate ordering minimizes the free‐energy penalty for segregation while preserving high configurational entropy, thereby promoting a balance that underpins high-temperature strength, environmental resistance, radiation tolerance, and cryogenic toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic or near-equiatomic Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy processed to yield a predominantly single-phase FCC disordered solid solution with a fine grain structure.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the Al content to induce controlled partial ordering that leads to formation of coherent B2 precipitates while keeping other processing parameters constant.
generation.conditions: Samples are fabricated under identical conditions (e.g., via directional solidification or controlled HPHT treatments similar to those in PMC11087546) and tested over a range of temperatures (from cryogenic to high-temperature) as well as under radiation and corrosive environments.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale, coherent B2 precipitates with very low lattice mismatch (e.g., mismatch factor ≈0.004) that are embedded in the disordered FCC matrix, forming a hierarchical microstructure.
generation.mechanism: A partial ordering driven by modest increases in Al content creates coherent phase interfaces that both reduce the thermodynamic driving force for deleterious phase separation and serve as effective sites for defect recombination and dislocation transmission. This synergy between high configurational entropy and controlled ordering stabilizes the phase and improves mechanical and environmental properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys within an optimal Al content range (likely near 14–21 at.% Al) will develop a defined volume fraction of coherent B2 precipitates that correlates with superior high-temperature strength, enhanced resistance to environmental degradation and radiation damage, and improved ductility and toughness at cryogenic temperatures relative to alloys that are either fully disordered or excessively ordered.
generation.baseline: An alloy exhibiting a single-phase FCC solid solution with minimal chemical ordering and no significant fraction of B2 precipitates.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to hold only within a moderate range of Al concentrations under processing conditions that maintain fine grain sizes and low residual stresses; it may not apply or may require adjustment in systems with significant additions of extra alloying elements (e.g., Ti) or under vastly different thermal histories.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative relationship between Al concentration, B2 phase volume fraction, and the resulting multi-environment property enhancements has not yet been established, and the optimal range of partial ordering remains to be defined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate a series of AlₓCoCrFeNi alloys with varying Al content (for example, 10, 15, 20, and 25 at.%) using an identical processing route that yields a fine-grained microstructure. Characterize the degree of ordering and precipitate morphology using X-ray diffraction and transmission electron microscopy. Subject the samples to high-temperature tensile tests, radiation (ion irradiation) experiments with subsequent TEM analysis, corrosion/oxidation studies, and cryogenic toughness tests. Analyze the correlation between Al content, the fraction and coherency of B2 precipitates, and the resultant mechanical and environmental properties.
measurements: X-ray diffraction for phase identification and quantification of ordering
Transmission electron microscopy to determine precipitate size, coherency, and lattice mismatch
Mechanical testing (tensile tests) at high and cryogenic temperatures
Ion irradiation followed by TEM for radiation damage assessment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If adjusting Al content does not produce a systematic variation in the degree of partial B2 ordering (e.g., measured by precipitate volume fraction and interfacial coherency) that correlates with consistent changes in high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, environmental resistance, and cryogenic toughness—such that no optimal range can be identified—then the hypothesis that partial ordering mediates phase stability in these HEAs will be considered falsified.

System: Al0.7CoCrFeNi (Al 14.8 Co 21.3 Cr 21.3 Fe 21.3 Ni 21.3 at. %). Processing: Homogenized alloy subjected to HPHT treatment at 6 GPa and 1473 K for 2 hours using a self-designed hexahedron-anvil-press apparatus. Test conditions: Uniaxial quasi-static tensile tests at room temperature with a strain rate of 3 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹.
